transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-19 10:00 PT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Jordan Patel, Liam O'Neill (Redwood); Aisha Rahman, Tom Keller, Priya Singh, Diego Marquez (Lunaris)

Summary (auto): weekly POC cost/econ review - focus on tokens/sec per dollar, caching, batching. Agreed benchmarks and data handoff.

00:00 Maya (AE): ok hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda - cost numbers, KV cache results, batching tradeoffs, next steps.
00:18 Aisha (Customer): thanks, yeah we mainly want to see end-to-end token cost and how caching affects our per-user bill - we have a lot of repeated prefixes across requests.
00:30 Jordan (SE): great. quick refresher: last week we ran a baseline on the hosted endpoint with gpt-ish open model, single-threaded, and got about 1,200 tokens/s per p4-like node, cost basis in sheet. note transcription: 'p4' may show up as 'pee four' in logs.
00:45 Tom (DevOps): we saw your sheet, question - is that tokens/sec/$ normalized for 8k context? ours is typically 2k average, 6k tail for some jobs.
01:02 Lydia (Speaker 2, misc): mhm
01:05 Jordan (SE): right so the baseline numbers assume 2k prompts avg but we also ran a 6k scenario. numbers change because inference time scales with sequence length for attention. our recommended config uses dynamic kernel selection and quantization which helps.
01:22 Aisha: can you restate tokens/sec per dollar in plain terms? customers want to compare to Anthropic and openai numbers.
01:30 Maya: sure - at current hosted pricing model the baseline model gives ~120k tokens per dollar for small-ctx workloads, with aggressive batching. with typical 2k average length and conservative batching to keep p95 under 350ms, that comes down to ~45k tokens/$ - big caveat is caching.
01:52 Priya (CTO): caching, yes - our traffic is 70% repeated initial prompts (templates). what's realistic savings from prefix or KV cache?
02:05 Jordan: in our internal tests, prefix/K-V cache saved 40-60% of token compute for workloads with ~70% repeat. we saw a 45% token compute reduction in the lightweight set. that maps to roughly a 30-40% cost reduction after network and orchestration overhead.
02:25 Diego (SRE): is that for hosted or dedicated? latency sensitivity matters.
02:29 Jordan: both; cache logic sits in the serving runtime so Dedicated or Hosted can use it. Dedicated gives more predictable throughput and we can pin cache hot-shards to GPUs to cut latency.
02:43 Tom: latency at p95 is our big blocker - we need <250ms p95 for user-facing UI. can you meet that at 50 RPS?
02:55 Liam (Solutions Eng): quick answer is yes for short contexts with batching tuned small; but long tail (6k contexts) will push p95 up. we recommend a hybrid routing policy: small/latency-sensitive requests -> low-latency pool (smaller batch window), large/throughput -> high-throughput pool with larger micro-batches.
03:15 Aisha: so batching helps cost but hurts latency. any concrete numbers?
03:22 Jordan: we did a sweep - small batch window (10ms) gave tokens/sec ~20k and p95 ~220ms. medium window (50ms) gave tokens/sec ~60k and p95 ~360ms. large window (200ms) gave tokens/sec ~150k but p95 up at ~700ms. depends on acceptance of p95.
03:45 Priya: interesting - so if we want sub-250ms p95, we need to keep batching small which drops tokens/$ by ~3x. caching helps but not enough alone.
03:58 Maya: exactly, caching reduces compute but you still pay some fixed request costs and networking. combined approach: modest batching (30-50ms) plus KV/prefix cache gave us the best cost/latency sweet spot in our tests.
04:12 Tom: can Dedicated reduce the tradeoff?
04:16 Jordan: Dedicated gives stable throughput and lower jitter; it doesn't change the fundamental batching vs latency curve but shifts it - for same p95 you can push higher tokens/sec because GPUs are reserved and hot caches are local. our internal number: Dedicated improved tokens/sec/$ by ~1.3x for this workload vs shared hosted.
04:36 Aisha: what about quantization - do we lose quality?
04:39 Liam: 4-bit quantization profiles we used had minor quality regressions on some open evals; for your templates we ran a small eval and didn't see regression above 95% pass. quantization improves throughput and reduces memory footprint enabling larger batch sizes.
04:58 Priya: ok. please show the final cost math end-to-end - tokens, compute, caching, network, storage.
05:05 Maya: yes we will update the cost_model_v2.xlsx with line items. I'll add an example scenario using your 70% repeat rate and 2k avg/6k tail.
05:18 Tom: about the benchmark - Jordan you mentioned a KV cache benchmark with 2k concurrent sessions?
05:23 Jordan: correct - we'll spin up a bench that replays your prompt distribution and measure effective tokens/s, p95, and cache hit rates. we'll also test different batch windows.
05:32 Aisha: for the bench we'll need you to use our sample dataset - we'll drop a link in the chat.
05:37 Maya: perfect, please upload to the shared drive and we'll use it. we'll also share the recording and the cost sheet after.
05:45 Diego: small note - security/compliance question: will Dedicated or Private require separate SOC2 docs? we may need to loop in legal.
05:53 Maya: yes, Private has separate legal and deployment docs. we will share security-soc2.pdf and SOC2 scope notes.
06:00 Priya: timeline - if bench looks good we may move to Dedicated pilot in April.
06:07 Maya: that fits. we'll aim to run the bench this week and demo Dedicated throughput next week.
06:15 Aisha: ok, anything else?
06:18 Jordan: one last thing - caching helps most when repeated prefixes are identical; if you rewrite prompts or add user-specific tokens at front, hit rate drops. check prompt design.
06:28 Aisha: noted.
06:30 Maya: recap of next steps - Maya shares cost sheet and links, Jordan runs bench + shares results, Aisha shares prompt distribution and dataset. schedule follow up for week of 2026-03-29.
06:45 Priya: thanks all.
06:47 Meeting end.

References/links mentioned: cost_model_v2.xlsx (drive link), KV-cache-benchmark plan (doc link), security-soc2.pdf (link), demo recording placeholder

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: 'K-V' written as 'KV' and sometimes 'prefix cache' transcribed as 'pre-fix cache' or 'pre-fix cash'. Speaker labels merged in a few spots.
